title: Inventory reorder point under normal demand and service level
scenario_markdown: Daily hospital demand for a critical surgical dressing kit follows a normal distribution with mean $\mu = 200$ kits and standard deviation $\sigma = 30$ kits ($X \sim N(200, 30^2)$). To prevent surgical cancellations while minimizing holding costs, the materials manager establishes a $90\%$ cycle service level, meaning inventory must be sufficient to satisfy total daily demand on at least $90\%$ of days ($P(X \le s) \ge 0.90$). What inventory stock $s$ must be on hand each morning, and what is the resulting daily stockout probability?
assumptions: Continuous normal distribution X ~ N(200, 30^2) in units
Independent daily demand draws without serial autocorrelation
Service level 0.90 corresponds to cumulative non-stockout probability P(X <= s) = 0.90

approval.notes: Reviewed inventory service level derivation: Z* for 90% service level is 1.28155 (table 1.28). Safety stock ss = 1.28155 * 30 = 38.45 kits. Total stock s = 200 + 38.45 = 238.45 kits. Daily stockout probability is 1 - 0.9000 = 0.1000. Excel NORM.INV(0.90, 200, 30) verified.
approval.delegation_basis: Content backlog Batch 1: Row 3.2 normal distribution expansion

stages.prompt_markdown: What standardized score $Z^*$ provides a $90\%$ cycle service level ($P(Z \le Z^*) = 0.90$)?

options.hint_markdown: A service level above $50\%$ requires carrying inventory above mean demand, which requires a positive $Z$-score.
$1.645$ corresponds to a $95\%$ service level, not a $90\%$ service level.
$0.90$ is the service level probability (cumulative area), not the number of standard deviations $Z$.

stages.explanation_markdown: A $90\%$ service level requires cumulative non-stockout probability $\Phi(Z^*) = 0.90$. Looking up $0.9000$ in standard normal tables gives $Z^* \approx 1.28$ (software gives $1.28155$). Excel formula: `=NORM.S.INV(0.90)`.

stages.prompt_markdown: Using $Z^* \approx 1.282$, what total inventory level $s = \mu + Z^* \sigma$ (expected demand plus safety stock $ss = Z^* \sigma$) must the hospital stock?

options.hint_markdown: Stocking only expected demand ($200$ kits) satisfies demand on only $50\%$ of days ($Z = 0$), resulting in a $50\%$ stockout probability.
Safety stock must be added as a buffer above expected demand, not subtracted.
A flat percentage buffer ignores demand volatility $\sigma = 30$. $220$ kits gives $Z = (220-200)/30 = 0.67$, achieving only a $74.8\%$ service level.

stages.explanation_markdown: Total stock consists of cycle stock (mean demand $\mu = 200$) plus safety stock ($ss = Z^* \sigma = 1.28155 \times 30 = 38.45\text{ kits}$): $s = 200 + 38.45 = 238.45\text{ kits}$ (or $238.4$ kits with table $Z = 1.28$). In practice, the hospital stocks $\lceil 238.45 \rceil = 239$ kits. Excel formula: `=NORM.INV(0.90, 200, 30)`.

stages.prompt_markdown: When maintaining this target stock level of $s = 238.45\text{ kits}$, what is the exact probability of experiencing a stockout on any given day ($P(X > 238.45)$)? Enter as a decimal or percentage rounded to four decimal places.
stages.explanation_markdown: A stockout occurs when daily demand exceeds stock on hand. By the complement rule: $P(X > s) = 1 - P(X \le s) = 1 - 0.9000 = 0.1000$ (or $10.00\%$). Excel formula: `=1 - NORM.DIST(238.45, 200, 30, TRUE)` or `=1 - NORM.S.DIST(1.2816, TRUE)`.
